persona.bio: Receptionist at a family dental office with two dentists. Phones all morning, booking and moving appointments, texting patients to reschedule when a dentist is out, checking insurance, reminding people about cleanings, and answering the same questions about parking, payment plans and what to bring. She texts patients from the office system and her work phone. Her office manager said AI is fine as long as no patient details go in. She tried ChatGPT twice for a letter.

path.role: You’re the receptionist at a dental office, handling phones, scheduling, insurance and patient messages.

steps.firstStep: I’m a receptionist at a dental office. I send patients text messages about appointments, including reminders and moved appointments. Write a short, friendly text message, two or three sentences, that is warm and clear and easy to read on a phone. Keep it to one message with no extra explanation. Here is what this one is about: [paste the details of this appointment here]

steps.note: I am a receptionist at a dental office. I handle phones, scheduling, insurance questions and patient messages. When I ask you to write something, it goes to patients, so keep it warm, calm and short. I like plain sentences and a friendly tone, and I usually want a text to be two or three sentences. Never add details I did not give you, like times, prices, coverage or policies. Use square brackets for anything I need to fill in. Never include private patient details. If you are not sure about something, ask me before you guess.

steps.title: Your reminder texts, saved once on your phone
steps.read: Your reminder texts now live on your phone’s keyboard. Each one is a few letters away, so you stop writing the same message from scratch many times a day. You read it, change the name or the time, and send it. That keeps every text steady and in your own voice.

material.label: Your reminder texts
items: Hi [first name], this is a reminder of your appointment on [day] at [time]. Reply here if you need to change it. Thanks!
Hi [first name], we are looking forward to seeing you on [day] at [time]. Please let us know if anything changes. Thanks!
Hi [first name], [dentist] is out on [day], so your appointment is moving to [new day and time]. Reply here if that does not work and I will find another slot. Thanks!
Hi [first name], we have not heard back about your appointment on [day] at [time]. Please reply to confirm, or call us if you need to move it. Thanks!
Hi [first name], we are sorry we missed you today. Reply here and I will help you find a new time. Thanks!
Hi [first name], a spot opened up on [day] at [time]. Reply here if you would like it and I will book it for you.

steps.title: Your recall reminders, saved once on your phone
steps.read: Recall reminders are added to the keyboard replies you set up for your reminder texts. They sit with the others, each a few letters away.

material.label: Your recall reminders
items: Hi [first name], it is time to schedule your next visit with us. Reply here or call [office phone] and we will find a time that works. Thanks!
Hi [first name], it has been a while since your last visit. Would you like to book your next appointment? Reply with a day that suits you and I will check the schedule.
Hi [first name], we still have your recall visit open. We have times on [day] and [day]. Reply with the one you prefer and I will book it.
Hi [first name], just checking in about your next visit. If you already booked, please ignore this message. If not, reply here and I will help you find a time.
Hi [first name], we would love to see you again. Reply here or call us to book your next visit. Thanks!

safeUse: Never type a patient’s name, date of birth, phone number or address into Claude. Use brackets and fill those in yourself.
Never type insurance member numbers, claim details or payment information.
Never paste notes from a patient chart or anything about a patient’s health.
Read every reminder text before you send it, and check the day and time against the schedule.
Keep insurance and coverage answers coming from your office’s own approved sources, not from a draft.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager name], I would like to know which AI tools the office approves and what I may use them for. I have two tasks in mind. One is writing appointment reminder texts and recall reminders, and the other is drafting answers to common phone questions. I would not type any patient names or private details into a tool, and I would read everything before it goes out. Could you tell me what is allowed, or point me to the right person?

design.today: You write these many times a day, often from scratch. A typical one is a short note like moving a 2pm visit to Thursday at 10 when Dr. Patel is out.
design.newWay: Your most common reminder and reschedule texts are saved on your phone, each a few letters away. You type the short code, fill in the day, time and name, read it and send it yourself. Every text keeps the same friendly wording, and you stop rewriting the same message from scratch.

steps.goal: List the four or five reminder and reschedule texts you send most, such as a plain reminder, a dentist out today move, and a confirm request.
Get ChatGPT ready on your phone and computer so you can draft the saved texts.
Turn your list into saved replies on your phone, each with gaps for the name, day and time.
Leave patient names, dates and health details out of anything you type into the AI tool, and fill them in only on your phone.

material.label: Reminder text set
material.what: Four or five short texts with gaps for the name, day and time, written in the tone of your example message.

material.label: Short codes
material.what: A list of the letters that bring up each saved text on your phone.

material.label: Reply line
material.what: One closing sentence that invites the patient to reply if the new time does not work.

design.checkPoint: You read each text and fill in every gap, then send it yourself.

design.today: You send these on a regular basis to bring patients back in.
design.newWay: One saved assistant holds your recall wording, so a draft with the right tone is ready whenever you need one. You paste in only a first name and the kind of visit, check the draft against your work system and send it from your usual tools. Your work email stays unconnected, and patient details stay in your own systems.

steps.goal: Get Claude ready on your computer so you can set up a saved assistant.
Make a project that holds your recall wording and instructions for each type of recall.
Set up the saved assistant so it writes a recall message from a first name and visit type only.
Decide which details you will never paste in, such as full names, birth dates, phone numbers and treatment records.

material.label: Assistant instructions
material.what: Tells the assistant to write short, warm recall messages for a dental office and to leave gaps for anything it does not know.

material.label: Recall wording
material.what: Sample messages for a six month cleaning, an overdue visit and a follow up after treatment.

material.label: Tone notes
material.what: Your plain, friendly style taken from your example message, including how you invite a reply.

design.checkPoint: You read each draft, check the patient and visit details in your work system, and send it yourself.
